In referring to Canada's definite offer he had this to say, as reported at page 3922 of Hansard:
We are producing the F-86E, the CF-100, the T-33 trainer, the latest Harvard type trainer, plus light transport aircraft-the Otter, the Beaver and the Chipmunk, leading aircraft of their type. As far as we know there is not anything to match them; and it is high time, I think, that the Canadian people began to recognize that their air force has become one of the leading air forces in effective fighting power on our side today.
The then minister of national defence recognized in that statement that aircraft, even light aircraft, adds to one's potential; and the importance of aircraft varies a great deal, of course, with the situation. Of course, a Chipmunk or a Beaver aircraft, or aircraft of similar types, would be sitting ducks if they were to operate against perhaps Sabres or some other type of modern jet-propelled aircraft, but they are very formidable weapons if they are operating against stray patrols on a desert who have no adequate means of protecting themselves against aircraft. As a matter of fact some of these similar types are ideal for that sort of thing.
Then aircraft can take on special importance, even obsolescent types of aircraft, or small transport aircraft, under certain conditions. During the last war the R.A.F. found it necessary, when the threat of invasion was very great and the means of defence very small, to prepare to use Tiger Moths and other very light training aircraft for offensive purposes against ground troops if an invasion came.
I seek clarification of the statement of the minister regarding this particular aircraft. The minister said the aircraft in question was a Chipmunk. I seek this information by the way. Since the minister himself is not in his seat, perhaps he might have notice given of it so that an answer can be forthcoming. I note that the item regarding that aircraft is listed as being in one case about $44,000, and in the other, about $41,000. That is approximately the price of a Beaver aircraft. I think a Beaver aircraft sells for $35,000 plus in this country depending on what equipment is on it; and a Chipmunk, which is the other aircraft, costs about $25,000 in this country. I should like to have an explanation of the great difference in price.

Shipment of Arms Abroad
In the course of the questions and answers on the orders of the day over the last two days, it would appear there has been an attempt on the part of the government to belittle our exports of arms and other warlike material in certain cases because they are obsolete, or the items themselves are small, or the quantity is not great. This makes little sense to me. What the government is saying in effect when such exports go to sensitive areas is that we are only tossing small sparks into the powder keg. I would like to point out that under certain circumstances even small contributions of lethal weapons can be very aggravating to the persons on whom they are used.
I am speaking only from memory in this case but I believe it was the Prime Minister who recently said that when export permits were asked for, great consideration was given to the situation and an endeavour was made to ensure that the export would not upset the balance of power between two of these minor countries, and therefore there would be no danger of their engaging in an arms race. It would seem to me there might be occasions when we might believe the power as between two nations was in balance, but I think it would be an extremely difficult task to convince them, if they were in balance, to stay that way. I am sure if a small nation with aggressive or belligerent tendencies were do learn that its power was in balance with its would-be victim, it would not be satisfied *with that situation and would make every effort to get the balance upset in its own favour as quickly as possible.
Even if it were possible to maintain perfect balance as between two small countries, what is the objective? Is it to keep them in a state of tension, sniping at each other indefinitely in an indecisive way until they eventually attain the condition of the Kilkenny cats? What is the motive? There is great danger that a small war may spread and involve the whole civilized world. In this day of the atom bomb such an event would be absolutely fatal to our civilization, in all probability, if a full scale war were waged.
I therefore think this theory is completely <unsound; it is much akin to using the argument that if you see two small boys fighting in the street and the little fellow is getting the worst of the deal, you should furnish him -with a brick in order that he might try to knock out the bigger fellow's brains. That does not make sense to me. I think what is required is a firm, honest approach to the situation. The boys should be chastised and if necessary the police should be called.
That, I think, is the situation today as far as small belligerent nations are concerned.


After all, the United Nations was set up as an organization in an attempt to find a means of resolving differences between nations by means other than war and force.
I believe it has been said in this house that if we were to refuse arms shipments to a small nation, we might be endangering its existence by withholding from it its ability to defend itself. In that regard I should like to point out that the United States appears to be of the same opinion as I am with regard to the two small boys. Just the other day the government of the United States turned down a request from Israel for a shipment of $50 million worth of arms on the grounds that such a shipment would not be in the interests of the maintenance of peace in the area concerned, but rather that such a shipment would further endanger peace in that area. If war is to be prevented it must be prevented by the existence of a force which can compel small nations who are bickering among themselves to come to the conclusion that they must resort to reasonableness and compromise to settle their differences.
I think, Mr. Speaker, we cannot further Canada's interests and retain for Canada the enviable position it has attained in world affairs if we renounce our ideals and our principles for some minor convenience for somebody. I believe that in the end ideals are still of greater consequence and value than are bombs, even than atom bombs under some circumstances.
This cabinet includes men, I believe, who would like to be looked upon, or who would like to think they are looked upon, as world statesmen. This is the opportunity for them to prove their worth. An amendment has been proposed asking that the whole question of the export of arms on the part of Canada be thoroughly examined so the facts may be revealed. If we have the facts we can then determine where we should go and what action should be taken. If this government is made up of men of good will I think they will welcome such a committee. They will see in it the opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities in dealing with these matters of world importance.
I think the Canadian people at this time demand a frank, forthright statement as to what is the situation. The Canadian people do not want truculence on the part of their ministers, they want candor. The Canadian people rightly demand that they have the right to work out their own destiny. Not only do they want to know where they are going, they want to know to where they may be led. I am quite sure the vast majority of the Canadian people have had no idea that Canada was

exporting arms and munitions of war to areas other than NATO and commonwealth countries. I think it is only reasonable to ask that the Canadian people should be made fully aware of what the code of conduct shall be for Canada when considering the export of arms or munitions of any sort to any part of the world.
If this government is made up of men of good will they will welcome this opportunity, they will welcome the assistance which representatives of the people would be able to give them in trying to find a means of controlling the export of arms so that such export will work to the benefit of the Canadian people and for the cause of peace. They should be glad that we are seeking the facts; they should be glad that an opportunity is being given for merit to be recognized, for errors to be corrected and for objectives to be attained.
If they wish to prove themselves men of good will they will accept this amendment knowing that it will provide an opportunity for them to demonstrate if not their efficiency at least their high motives. Naturally I assume that the members of the government are men of good will; as a matter of fact I guess I have no other choice. This is essentially a problem of external affairs, and the conduct of a maturing nation in world affairs is vital to the Canadian people. If Canada with the growth of its strength is to retain the high position it has held in the councils of the world we must be sure that we act in the interests not only of ourselves and of our allies but of peace as well.
I am happy to support the amendment which has been moved, and I hope it will be accepted by the government. By doing so they will demonstrate that they are men of good will. I believe completely that on earth there shall be peace to men of good will.

Mr. Speaker, this whole question of the sale of arms, munitions and equipment of war is of course closely tied up with the whole matter of disarmament. Last fall I had the pleasure of being a parliamentary observer at the tenth general assembly of the United Nations and sitting in at all the meetings of the disarmament conference. Anyone who has had that opportunity I think will realize fully the difficulties of the problem of disarmament. World disarmament cannot be achieved very easily, but I think the general observation can be made that the indiscriminate sale of arms, particularly to trigger-happy tribesmen and others, will do nothing to further improve world peace. I certainly think that Canada,
Shipment of Arms Abroad which is so highly respected among other countries, should set an example in this regard.
This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre moved the following amendment:
That, in the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, ammunition, and military equipment. should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.
That amendment naturally brings two questions to mind. First, assuming that a code of procedure is needed, why have the proposed committee recommended such a code of procedure? Second, why is a code of procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, munitions and military equipment needed at all?
With respect to the first question, apparently there is no procedure at the present time with regard to the issuing of export permits for arms and other military equipment. This has become quite obvious since the opening of this session from the answers that have been received to questions asked. Apparently we can expect that sometimes the government makes these decisions, while on other occasions, as the Prime Minister indicated this afternoon, the decisions are purely ministerial and nothing else.
This proposed committee, which I hope will be set up, should certainly formulate a code of procedure so that hon. members can find out, in camera if necessary, the quantities shipped, their destinations, the controls over the shipment of arms and the reasons for the shipments. I am sure that Canadians generally do not wish this country to be regarded by other countries as a merchant of death. If we are going to sell arms I think the reasons for selling them should be carefully considered.
This code of procedure should set out controls over the ultimate destination of arms. Arms may apparently be going to country A but it may be quite possible that they will end up in country B. Third, and most important of all, this procedure should be such as to assure that all ministers of the crown are informed of what arms sales are being approved.
My second question is, why should there be a special procedure necessary for the sale of arms? Arms are a very special commodity; they are not like apples, potatoes, wheat, fish or anything like that. The sale of arms to other countries could very well alter longterm government policy or even short-term government policy toward such countries or toward related countries. There can be

Shipment of Arms Abroad nothing but confusion if one minister permits the sale of arms without the other ministers knowing about it, particularly if the policy toward the government that may be affected by the sale is the responsibility of ministers who are not informed about the sale.
Since I have come to this house I have heard the government referred to as acting in such a way that the one hand does not know what the other hand is doing. I do not know that that is a suitable metaphor and I think we should go back to ancient times, to Greek mythology, to find a more suitable comparison. One of the labours of Hercules was to slay a creature called the Hydra or better known as the seven-headed serpent. This was a creature with one body and seven heads all going in different directions, and one not knowing what the other ones were doing.
That is the government.
They have seven bodies and one head.

It might be better, in view of the remarks of my hon. friend, to have seven bodies and one head rather than one body and seven heads going in different directions. I should like to give a few illustrations of the point I have just made. First of all, the sale of arms can affect the long-range policies of the government. I think there is very little question about the fact that the general long-range policy of this government is to maintain world peace. That is what we have been told in this house and outside it. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the London Free Press, week end magazine edition, for January 28, 1956. This is an article entitled "This is our Foreign Policy" by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On page 2 of this edition the article states, referring to Canada:
We are respected because we try to play a constructive and conciliatory role in international affairs.
Continuing a little further, it states on page 3:
We are respected also because we have not hesitated to accept our share of the burden of maintaining peace and promoting friendship between peoples; in the United Nations, in NATO, and elsewhere.
A little further on it states:
That, in fact, is the aim of our foreign policy: to play our full part in collective action for peace and in the search for solutions to the problems that now so dangerously divide the world.
It would seem to me that the sale of arms to the countries in the Caribbean, as referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and elsewhere, can hardly bring about such conciliation and conciliatory measures.


More important, these approvals of the sale of arms by one minister of the crown when the others are apparently unaware of it, in effect are short-term policies toward various countries.
The same article to which I have already referred in a box on page 4, stated the policy of this government toward Israel and the Arab countries, as follows:
We have had requests in the past-in the last few years-from both Israel and Egypt and other Arab states. Our attitude is to do nothing that would disturb the military balance-
Here is what might be called the punch line:
-or add to their offensive strength.
This is an article written by the Secretary of State for External Affairs laying down government policy with respect to Israel and the Arab States. It says that the policy is to add nothing to their offensive strength; yet we have had admissions this year of the approval of sales of arms to those countries. There is hardly any consistency in that.
For these reasons we must have a code of procedure with respect to the sale of arms, even if it does nothing more than inform all ministers of the crown as to what arms are being shipped to other countries. The present slipshod, slap-happy method of doing things can only lead, as it has already, to disintegration of government policy. You might say that the present policy is simply an illustration of "I don't know where I'm going but I'm on my way."
Mr. Speaker, I intend my remarks to be very brief, but they will not be as brief as three minutes. I do not know whether to call it ten o'clock.
No.
Ten o'clock.

Apparently there is not consent. I have been interested in this debate and have been asking myself, if the government is not prepared to agree to this, why that can be so. I would like to read the resolution to remind the house what is in it, how simple it is and how obvious is its good sense. The amendment is:
That, In the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, ammunition, and military equipment, should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.
The first question that arises is as to whether there is now a definite code of procedure. I would think any member in this house and, most of all, any member of the government

would be quick to agree that there is no definite code of procedure. I was going to say that at best there was a hodgepodge of understandings among ministers, but I think that would be a great exaggeration. I think I should say "a hodgepodge of misunderstandings", because we never seemed to get to the point where there was an understanding among the ministers. We had an interesting galaxy of ministers parading before us- the minister of external affairs, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of National Defence-and we got an interesting glimpse of the way they communicate with each other. I am reminded of the Prime Minister, but I omitted the Prime Minister because I think he was as innocent of the whole matter as a new born babe.

They do not tell him what is going on.

I doubt if he even heard any of the echoes that reverberated from department to department.
They never tell the boss.

That being so I come back to my first suggestion, that the government should be very glad indeed to have a definite code of procedure, and that a very sensible way of getting it would be the method suggested in this resolution.
Mr. Speaker, if my eyes tell me rightly it is ten o'clock. As the rest of my speech contains a few suggestions as to the only possible reasons the government could have for not agreeing to this, perhaps the government would be more interested in hearing them tomorrow.
On motion of Mr. Macdonnell the debate was adjourned.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Monday, February 6, 1956, at 2.30 p.m.
Sir Anthony Eden was introduced by Mr. St. Laurent.
Hon. L. Rene Beaudoin, Speaker of the House of Commons, presided.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister of Canada):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons, fellow members of parliament, it is my agreeable duty and privilege to welcome to the Canadian parliament the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. This I do with warm personal pleasure, and I know that all members share that pleasure and wish me to express on their behalf, as well as my own, our most cordial greetings to our distinguished guest.
We were all delighted, sir, when we learned that it would be possible for you to spend a few days in our capital following your important discussions in Washington, and that you had graciously accepted to speak to us here this afternoon.
I should like also to say how happy we are that the foreign secretary, Right Hon. Selwyn Lloyd, was able to accompany you on this visit. To him as well we extend a sincere and hearty welcome.
We recall, Mr. Prime Minister, that you previously addressed this parliament some 13 years ago when we were emerging from the darkest and most dangerous days of the war. The might of the enemy forces was still great, but the dawn of ultimate victory was beginning to appear.
Those of us who were here have vivid recollections of the inspiring message of courage and confidence you brought us from the battle-scarred but indomitable British nation.
You were then the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs in a wartime government headed by one of the great Englishmen of historical fame, that towering figure, Sir Winston Churchill, to whom the whole free world will remain forever indebted.
Today we welcome you as the worthy successor in office of that great man, and we do 67509-58
so on the morrow of your visit to Washington where you have been strengthening Anglo-American co-operation and friendship, the essential foundation for the structure of peace which we are all striving to build.
May we be permitted to congratulate you on the success of that mission? Of course, I do not need to tell you that whenever London and Washington and Paris seek to deepen their friendly understanding, there is a feeling of very special satisfaction in Ottawa.
That visit to Washington was only another instance of the energetic, skilful and constructive part which you have played in international affairs during these troubled and trying years.
Your visit to us emphasizes the close association we enjoy with the United Kingdom and the other members of our commonwealth of nations. That association, based on the freedom of its members, spans the oceans and the continents; it is playing a worthy part in the search for peace, security and constructive progress.
We are also proud of our association with the United Kingdom as allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and as fellow members of the United Nations. In these organizations, too, we appreciate the opportunities of working with you for the strengthening of the free world and the maintenance of peace.
(Translation):
Mr. Prime Minister, you know that there are in Canada, and in this parliament, two official languages. And so I wish to tell you, on behalf of Canadians of French descent like myself, how happy they are also to greet you here and to extend to you a most hearty welcome.
I am conscious of accurately expressing the feelings of my fellow Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific when I say that they have the very highest regard for you.

Address by Sir Anthony Eden
(.Text):
I now invite Right Hon. Sir Anthony Eden, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, to address us.
Righl Hon. Sir Anthony Eden (Prime Minister of the United Kingdom): Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons, members of the Senate and of the House of Commons, Mr. Prime Minister, I am indeed grateful to you, sir, for your generous words, and to the Canadian parliament for this invitation. I am deeply moved by the compliment which you have paid to me for the second time in my life. That must be a rare event. I believe that it is in fact unique in history. On neither occasion, Mr. Speaker, have I been able to catch your eye. I do trust the backbench members will not in consequence be so much aggrieved that they will move the closure on me. I was a little reassured to learn, sir, that this is an unusual custom for your parliament.
You know that I speak sincerely when I say I am happy to be amongst you again. It is now 30 years since I first came to Canada and travelled across your country. On many occasions since then I have had opportunities to visit your vast and hospitable land. I am proud to think that I have more friends here than in any country outside my own.
(Translation):
French-speaking Canadians, I thank you cordially for your welcome. I do wish to say how much I admire and respect that culture and those traditions you so proudly preserve. You know that I am genuinely glad to be amongst you again. Thirty years have elapsed since my first visit to Canada. I have returned several times to your vast and hospitable land and, on each occasion, I have found many old friends and have made new ones.
I am deeply grateful for the high honour you have paid me in inviting me, for the second time in my life, to address the Canadian parliament.
(Text) :
Inevitably, my mind goes back this afternoon to that earlier occasion, to which you, Mr. Prime Minister, have referred, when I spoke to you during the war. Then, though the tide had turned, victory had yet to be won and the future beyond it lay all uncertain. He would be a rash man or an ill-informed man who would attempt a confident prophecy for mankind today.
Yet there is a certain balance sheet of good and evil which we can draw up, and I propose to do so, and to begin with the good, because it is more comforting that way. There is next the unshakable strength of

the Anglo-American alliance in which we all join. Third, the growing unity of western Europe within the framework of NATO. Fourth, and grimmer but still real, the deterrent power of the new weapons, including the hydrogen bomb, which restrain where they cannot reform. Fifth, the growing understanding by the west of the threat of communist penetration which it has to meet and of the new methods which we will have to employ.
And now on the debit side I would cite, first, the increasing hazards which some are prepared to take; second, the dangers of aggression by countries which believe they can ignore the deterrent; third, the continued existence of local disputes, whose consequences could engulf the world; fourth, the daily communist call to abhor the west sounds sharply. In contrast, the steady effort of the west to raise the standard of life for all free people must take time. It is easier to spread hatred than to make two blades of grass grow where one grew before.
Mr. Speakers, it is with this balance of good and evil in mind that we have to prepare ourselves. Economic weapons may take the place of military ones. But always our purpose must be the same; to maintain the right that men's minds may be free and the care that their bellies be filled. Well now, to achieve this, free nations like ourselves, like free men, must draw and hold together and it is in the spirit of those reflections that I would like to make some comments on the recent conversations which I have held in Washington with President Eisenhower.
I can best sum up my impressions of those talks by saying that there has never been so full a measure of agreement between our governments. In the whole field of European diplomacy, which a year or two back was troublesome enough, there was no difference between us. You may have noticed the attempts of the Kremlin to obscure the issues and confuse our councils. In fact they only provided most obligingly an opportunity to underline the unity between the United States and ourselves.
Now, Mr. Speaker, much of our meeting was devoted to the difficult and critical problems of the Middle East. Here too we were in agreement that the first danger was the continuing Arab-Israel dispute. We were also in agreement as to what we should do to try to resolve it. We decided that the necessary treatment should be of three kinds. We should continue to work without publicity-I really think diplomacy is more effective without publicity-and by every means to bring about a settlement in that area. This can only be realized if both sides are prepared to reconcile the positions they have taken up to now.

That means a compromise. Some people tell me compromise is a horrible English habit; however, some might learn from it to their own advantage in the world. But we can both help, and are ready to do so, for example by financial aid to help settle the tragic refugee problem and by a guarantee of the frontiers once agreed.
Meanwhile, as you know, Mr. Speaker, we, the United States and France have our responsibilities under the tripartite declaration of 1950. We arranged for discussions on the action to be taken to meet an emergency should it arise. The French government has agreed to join us in this. Personally I am convinced that to make ready in this way is to reduce the risk of conflict. It may also be, Mr. Speaker, that a strengthening of the United Nations truce supervisory organization would assist to prevent incidents. Both the United Kingdom and the United States governments are very ready to agree to this. But of course we should wish to be guided by General Burns, a brave Canadian soldier who is resolutely carrying out this thankless task.
As regards the dispute which we have with Saudi Arabia, our position is this. We are not prepared to return to arbitration. There can be no question of that in view of our recent experiences with their bribery and corruption. On the other hand, as we made clear in Washington, we are ready to enter into direct discussions.
The United States government has declared its solid support for the Baghdad pact, to which we belong. This again we welcome and here again our views are alike. The pact has economic purposes and aims which fully match its military provisions and importance. We have considered the kind of help which each member country needs and we are determined to make a success of the pact.
All this does not exclude some help to other countries in the area. An example is Jordan, to whom we shall continue to make substantial payments under our treaty.
So much then for what is perhaps the most critical region at the present time. Of course, we talked of many other problems, in many parts of the world, just as I had the privilege to do with the Prime Minister and your cabinet this morning. We discussed the declaration of Washington which the President and I issued together. In this we set forth the true principles which guide the free world. Some say that these have been stated before. Maybe, but it does no harm to state them again in a manner which makes it clear that we are aware of the modern communist challenge. The declaration of Washington is, in fact, a charter to which the whole of the free world can subscribe. I am sure that here in 67509-58J
Address by Sir Anthony Eden Canada you will agree with its purpose. It is in the tradition of the work you have done so well to unite the countries on either side of the Atlantic in defence of the free world.
Mr. Speakers, I now come back to our own friendship and the work of our two peoples together. Many speakers and writers have tried to define the commonwealth. None has really succeeded, for the reason no doubt that the spirit which gives it life is indefinable.
In a few months' time I look forward to welcoming the prime ministers of the commonwealth to our London meeting. Foremost amongst them is your own Prime Minister, wisest of counsellors and most loyal of friends. May I here suggest that though we enjoy being the hosts to all these meetings of prime ministers, it would be good if from time to time the meeting place were to revolve.
Mr. Speakers, I am here this afternoon surrounded by the familiar setting of our own House of Commons. This morning, Mr. Prime Minister, you were good enough to invite me and my colleague the foreign secretary to attend the Canadian cabinet. Our systems, our modes of thought, our traditions and our ways of life are all so much alike that perhaps we ought not to take too much credit to ourselves, but Anglo-Canadian relations are a model to the world.
But there is more to it than all this. The pervading influence which the commonwealth carries into the four corners of the earth is one of understanding among friends, of tolerance and of peace.
In all this work Canada now plays a leading part. It is impossible to travel, as I had to do as foreign secretary until a year ago, into so many lands without constantly hearing warm praise of the judgment and kindly help you have so often extended to "less happier lands". The service that you are rendering in Indo-China is but one example of the world's debt to you. By this action alone you made possible an armistice which may yet become a peace.
Mr. Speakers, if I may conclude on a slightly more familiar note, I have from my childhood, like many of you, seen this great nation grow up into a position where its authority is among the foremost in the world. I have no doubt of what the future holds. You will be called upon to carry ever more burdensome responsibilities, but they go with authority. That is inescapable. Yet ever so at home and over the world at large there is great comfort in that thought, for I have no doubt that the guidance and wisdom of Canada will always be thrown in the scales on the side of toleration and peace.

It is not given to many of us to look far into the future, but of this no one who observes your country from outside can doubt a future, an almost unimaginably great future, is in your hands. I have no doubt that you will fashion it in a manner worthy of a great people.
And so, Mr. Speakers, I salute this Canada which commands the future as probably no other land in the world today. I salute you also as the standard bearer of loyalty and a herald of good will. And I wish you well.

On behalf of the Senate of Canada may I say to you, Mr. Prime Minister, how greatly we appreciate your visit to Canada, your courtesy in meeting with us and, on their behalf, may I thank you for the address you have just delivered.
We will never forget the gigantic effort and sacrifice that the people of the United Kingdom made in the cause of freedom; their contribution in the rebuilding of a war-torn world and their efforts in building a better future.
The attendant circumstances of your visit, Mr. Prime Minister, are evidence of the leadership you are continuing to show in this respect. I need hardly say that in the peculiar position Canada occupies in relation in particular to the United Kingdom and the United States and, in general, to the other countries that are signatories to the North Atlantic treaty, we welcome every effort that is made towards greater understanding and in the achieving of a common viewpoint. Your very presence here and in Washington is evidence that you are keenly alive to the inestimable value of personal contacts in helping to attain these ends.
We would particularly ask you, Mr. Prime Minister, to convey our greetings to the members of the United Kingdom parliament. We hold them in the greatest respect, but we see far too little of each other. If it were possible to develop something more of the personal relationship and understanding between the members of our respective legislatures that already exist and are being constantly developed between the executive and administrative branches of government, not only would the attendant benefit be inestimable but it is quite possible that the difficulties of those whose responsibility it is to initiate policies might be lessened accordingly.
We wish you well in your undertakings. May divine Providence bless your endeavours.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Honoured guests, Mr. Prime Minister, hon. members of the Senate,

hon. members of the House of Commons, ladies and gentlemen:
(Translation) :
Once a well-known American writer, Nicholas Murray Butler, pointing out the multitudinous problems peculiar to the twentieth century, stressed the high ability required of the men called upon to solve those problems. Then again, another distinguished American author, Whittier, said: "Each crisis brings its words and deeds".
These words naturally come to mind at this time when it is my very great privilege to thank you, Mr. Prime Minister, for your interesting speech and your kindly presence among us. May I be allowed to add that the success of your career arouses in us the deepest admiration.
I should fear to lapse into the commonplace in repeating that Sir Anthony Eden, "the specialist in foreign affairs, the virtuoso of diplomacy", to use the words of his biographer, Campbell-Johnson, is a statesman of the highest intellectual standing who has always shown supreme ability and understanding in tackling the most difficult international problems.
At the general elections, in 1950, he summed up his political creed by referring to the theory of the three unities; first, the unity that should exist within the commonwealth; second, the unity of western Europe; and third, the unity which, across the Atlantic, binds England to the United States. Today he has restated his political faith in those three unities and has added two others which are most important and inseparable from the first three.
We believe, as he does, in maintaining a friendly solidarity between the countries which make up the commonwealth.
For us, who are French-speaking and whose mother country was France, we cannot forget, sir, that you have always been a friend of that great nation, that you have, on many occasions, revived the principles that made a success of the Entente Cordiale. You have always believed that the solidarity of Anglo-French relations, nay of western European relations, was the very basis of relations between all western European countries, not only for the present but also for the future.
There are, of course, "other places under the sun" and, as a North American people, we rejoice at your relations with the United States. On the occasion of your visit to America in 1943, President Roosevelt was able to say that you both seemed to agree on approximately ninety-five per cent of the

problems, which is a remarkable proportion. And in the last few days, you and the present President of the United States have just agreed one hundred per cent on the definition of the philosophy behind our way of life, as you personally chose to call it, a definition which was incorporated in this henceforth memorable document, the declaration of Washington.
This is consistent with the objective which is yours today and which you set yourself a long time ago when you said in the House of Commons:
I am convinced that a closer understanding between our nation and the United States constitutes the most important objective that the government of that country could propose to us.
Visit of Sir Anthony Eden
In addition you have accomplished a tour de force, as it were, in bringing about an effective rapprochement with new Germany.
As I said just now, each crisis brings its words and deeds, and brings forth the indispensable men whose courage and logic carry ideals into the realm of reality.
(Text) :
Each crisis brings its words and deeds; it' brings also to the fore the men to utter those words and to do those deeds, and men with sufficient courage and consistency to translate their ideals into realities. Of such a breed is our honoured guest today.
So, in the name of the House of Commons and of the Canadian people, may I say to you, sir: Thank you and good luck!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 31 the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) asked me whether the recommendations of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission for the 1956 sockeye salmon fishing regulations had been received. I replied that the recommendations had not been received but that when they were received a report would be made to the house.
The recommendations of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission have now been received in the department and are being studied. The recommendations ask that, for conservation reasons during the 1956 season, the area generally referred to as Juan de


Fuca straits be closed to salmon net fishing from June 28 to August 5 inclusive and that such closure be made effective under authority of the Fisheries Act in so far as Canadian nationals are concerned. The commission has recommended similar action to the government of the United States regarding United States nationals on the American side of Juan de Fuca straits, the regulations to be made effective under the legislation of the state of Washington.
The commission also proposes to prohibit salmon net fishing in outside waters, that is west of a line from Bonilla point to Tatoosh island for both Canadian and American fishermen. This latter regulation is made by the commission itself under the provisions of the international sockeye salmon convention.
The commission's recommendations regarding closure of the Juan de Fuca straits area are being studied by officials of the department and an announcement will be made in due course. Salmon net fishing in the area in question does not normally commence until the latter part of June.

Shipment of Arms Abroad Her Majesty's loyal opposition to raise a matter of importance and draw to the attention of the house a subject which, in the opinion of the opposition, deserves serious consideration.
For the last several weeks we have been considering some matters pertaining to the procedure followed by the government in dealing with the shipment abroad of military equipment, and a number of questions have been asked from time to time in order to obtain information. Some confusion has arisen with regard to the method and procedure followed in the shipment of military equipment from this country, not only in the minds of the members of this house but perhaps across the country, and there may even be some confusion in the minds of some members of the cabinet.
It would be interesting to clear up some of the terms that have been used from time to time in reference to the shipment of arms, ammunition and military equipment, such as orders in council, ministerial orders, ministerial decisions, export permits, and terms of that nature. I intend to move a motion to the effect that this matter be turned over to a committee of the house. At this stage I shall read but will not move the motion which will form the basis for the debate, and on which I hope to base my argument. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, ammunition, and military equipment, should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.
The value of suggesting reference to the external affairs committee is that expedition will result from that method of procedure. That committee is well able, from its experience, to deal with a matter of this sort.
Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but ignorance of government policy and administrative procedures might be used as an excuse for a person's lack of knowledge of what is going on, because government policy is sometimes obscure, sometimes in a state of flux, and sometimes it remains unknown unless intensive investigation is carried on, or some accident occurs.
During the course of the last several weeks we have been endeavouring to obtain information with regard to this matter I have raised. We have uncovered confusion. To every member of this house examples will occur of answers which lead to various interpretations, answers which are only partial replies to the questions asked, and answers which appear not to be answers at all. I propose using as an example three questions
[Mr. Churehill.l
that I asked in the house dealing with three matters concerning which I thought we should have information. My first question is found at page 525 of Hansard. It was addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and referred to mutilated gun barrels and breech blocks. I wanted to know whether those mutilated gun barrels and breech blocks were, if or when they were exported as scrap, beyond repair. Here is the minister's answer:
The instructions to the disposal corporation are that before guns are scrapped, and before they leave the possession of the corporation, the breech blocks are to be demolished. In other words, they are mutilated beyond repair.
That was a reply to half my question. I was much more interested in gun barrels, and to that part of the question no reply has been forthcoming. A mutilated gun barrel, in army parlance, is one which is not beyond repair. When sent to an armourer it can be put back in shape rather quickly. Is there any use in my asking now of the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether or not during the year 1955, or the preceding year, mutilated gun barrels have been exported from Canada as scrap metal? In all probability I would get a reply to the effect that no scrap metal had been shipped from Canada last week, and I would be no further ahead.
My second question concerned the extent of our traffic in arms, ammunition and military supplies. I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs, at page 521 of Hansard, whether or not we had sent any military equipment to any South American country in the last two years. This is the reply of the minister as recorded at page 557 of Hansard:
The answer is, no permits were issued for guns, ammunition, or military weapons of any kind, or for military aircraft or military vehicles to South America.
Does that mean that no military equipment was shipped to South America? Can military equipment be shipped without permits? I am at a loss to know what the answer means. I would place opposite that answer in Hansard the information which I obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics, which shows that during the year 1954, and for the ten months of 1955, military equipment to the amount of $63,980 was shipped to Peru, Ecuador, Uruguay and Venezuela. I took extreme care, and I checked the atlas. I found that after all these years these countries are still in South America. The headings in the dominion bureau of statistics return are: "Guns, rifles and other firearms; cartridges, gun and rifle."

My third question, addressed to the same minister, had reference to the shipment of military equipment to the 34 sensitive areas he had mentioned earlier, with the exception of Israel and Egypt. His reply indicated that $1 million worth of military equipment had gone during the last two years to sensitive areas outside the British commonwealth but he felt unable to give the names of the areas to which that equipment had been sent, although I asked for the names of those areas. It occurs to me that it is possible that a committee sitting in camera would be given that information so the picture would be entirely clear. It is because of answers like that, and because of the even more confusing answers we have heard in response to other questions, that I am suggesting this whole matter be referred to a committee which could seriously attempt to unravel the skein of confusion which prevails with regard to the entire question of exports of arms, ammunition and military equipment.
It seems to me that in matters of this sort the government follows a course of concealment, and when the truth appears to have been discovered it is followed by a denial such as the one which said in effect that no planes had been sent to Egypt and no arms to South America. This is followed by certain grudging admissions when pressed, and if the matter is pursued further it culminates in certain guilty disclosures. At that stage panic sets in and a smoke screen is thrown up to confuse the issue completely, and the fall-out extends from coast to coast. Of course, at that stage it is also customary to blame the opposition for not having raised the question on some other earlier occasion when the matter might have been considered and the information given by the government.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what are we doing about the shipment of arms, ammunition and military equipment overseas? Unless we can bring this matter before a committee and make a diligent search into it we will not know exactly what is being done. We have been told that there is no prohibition concerning shipments to our allies in NATO or to the commonwealth countries, but that there is a prohibition in relation to the Sino-Russian bloc. The question then arises concerning shipments to other countries outside of those areas, and it is with regard to those other countries outside of NATO and the British commonwealth that I was in complete ignorance of the fact that we were engaging in commercial transactions involving arms and general military equipment.
We have had pointed out to us in this rather purple fringe area of activity that
Shipment of Arms Abroad careful steps are taken to prevent any weapons going overseas that should not go, and things of that nature. Even today we were assured by the Prime Minister that in lifting the embargo the government was following the same policy as in the past. If I interpreted his words correctly they were to the effect that military equipment was not being shipped out of Canada to these countries of a nature that would encourage an arms race or be an incentive to aggression.
So we are informed that an elaborate control system has been set up; that such matters have to go before the cabinet and go through a procedure before three cabinet ministers; that various checks are involved that would secure Canada's position. The phrases used such as "consideration at cabinet level", "special care with regard to sensitive areas", "shipments only to defence departments", "assurances against re-export", "estimates of legitimate defence requirements of the receiving countries", "very special care that there is no temptation to commit aggression by the receiving country", indicate a very cautious approach indeed, as if the government realized that it was dealing with something of considerable significance to the people of Canada, as indeed it is.
But does the system work? It is only through an examination by a committee that we can find out whether or not that system does work. There is an escape clause-at least it is a confusing clause or phrase-in some of the information we have been given. The words used were, "shipments of any significance". We are told that such shipments have to go through the procedure that has been outlined. However, the words "any significance" have not been defined. What do they mean? Do they refer to the type of material that has been shipped or to the quantity or the value? We have not been told.
Another interesting question is, who makes the decision as to whether a shipment of military equipment is or is not significant? We are not informed with regard to that aspect of the question either. All arrows point to the minister in charge of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence also bear some responsibility with regard to this matter.
At this point, in order that we may be reassured the cloak of righteousness is thrown over the shoulders of the cabinet. If only we knew the number of orders that had been received for jet planes and the alacrity with which the cabinet turned down those orders.

Shipment of Anns Abroad If only we knew the total value of equipment that has been ordered and refused. The government has been tempted and has resisted temptation.
Well, that may be very reassuring to some people but I am not sure whether it will be reassuring to the hon. members of this house. Then we are told that after all no great quantities have been shipped, and also that the weapons that have been shipped are not' modern and dangerous.
Only a committee could find out the facts with regard to the procedure in the shipping of military equipment overseas to those countries outside NATO and the British commonwealth. How can we obtain that information in the house? That subject deserves intensive study.
There is a great danger in thinking that simply because great weapons of massive destruction have been developed over the last several years, weapons of so-called conventional design are not dangerous. It is wrong to think that simply because we are not shipping abroad atom and hydrogen bombs, jet planes, rockets and guided missiles and tanks, that we are shipping weapons that are not dangerous. Thinking in those terms you can reach the point where you think in effect that to kill men by obsolete and conventional weapons is not as objectionable as it is to kill them by modern means of mass destruction. We have it on the word of a person who heretofore has been considered competent to express opinions along those lines, and I would like t'o read the following words to the house:
We hope that atomic weapons will never be used. We also hope that machine guns and howitzers will not be used. The danger is that the uncritical acceptance throughout the world of the reprehensible quality of atomic weapons as such, rather than of violence itself, may lead to an assumption that the use of "conventional" weapons to kill men in order to achieve political objectives is somehow not so objectionable. A man is equally dead if killed by a bullet, an arrow or an atomic blast. It is the use of force that is to be condemned, not the physical source of that force.
Those words come from a book entitled 'Democracy in World Politics" of which I think the author is the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). Yet here le would have us believe that conventional weapons such as those we are disposing of are lot modern and dangerous.
I would hope that the committee investigat-ng this subject would consider our method if procedure, and in doing so find out what ;ypes of material were shipped overseas and whether or not we were sending modern and iangerous weapons. The purpose of weapons such as aeroplanes, tanks, guns, machine guns and rifles is to deliver upon the enemy an


explosive charge or a bullet which will destroy or kill. A jet aeroplane without ammunition is not as useful as a helicopter and a tank without ammunition is not as useful to an army as a bulldozer. It is the ammunition which is the important factor along with the weapon.
In the first world war artillery and mortar fire killed thousands of men and machine gun fire killed tens of thousands. Machine guns dominated the battlefield until their power was broken after four years of static warfare by the invention and use of the tank. In the second world war more powerful weapons of destruction were invented and used, but many thousands of men fell before the fire of machine guns and rifles. The V-l and V-2 were used toward the latter part of the war, but their destruction of civilian property and installations was not particularly important from the standpoint of the armies in the field.
Reporting in the latest issue of XJ.S. News and World Report, General Gruenther indicates that even if nuclear weapons are used there will still be need for armies to continue the use of conventional weapons. So how can you say they are not modern and dangerous? Therefore I submit that shipments of ammunition from this country to countries outside of NATO or other than countries which are our allies should be carefully examined. In what way are the permits issued? What controls are exercised to see that this ammunition does not get into the wrong channels?
An examination of the bureau of statistics report shows that in the last eight years Canada has shipped $800,000 worth of ammunition to Central America, the islands of the Caribbean and portions of South America. That would buy millions of rounds for rifles and machine guns. Why has Canada been shipping this type of material to areas which have nothing to do with us from the standpoint of our NATO alliance? What controls are exercised? Why are these shipments made? Is Canada entering into a traffic that represents an arms race and provides an incentive to aggression?
I notice that in 1949 over $20,000 worth of ammunition was shipped to the Dominican Republic. Why should the Dominican Republic want that amount of ammunition? I discovered that at that time that country feared an invasion from some of its neighbours and conferred upon its president full power to declare war. Consequently they needed ammunition. The adjoining neighbours whom they feared were Costa Rica, Panama and Cuba. Following its policy of balancing sides, of providing material to both sides so that

peace would be preserved, we find that Canada shipped about $40,000 of ammunition to those three areas.
Then I notice that in 1951 Cuba received over $100,000 worth of ammunition, and another $50,000 worth in 1952. What purpose was served by these shipments? Who issued the export permits? Were the needs and requirements of this country examined? We are told that extreme care is taken to determine the defensive requirements of a country, to see that the balance is not upset one way or another. What was going wrong in Cuba in 1951? The record shows that in the spring' of 1952 the government of Cuba was overthrown. An officer obtained control of the army, and with all that ammunition handy he was able to unseat the government. At the same time there apparently was no threat from the neighbouring countries, so Canada did not supply a great deal, except the customary $13,000 worth of ammunition to Costa Rica.
Then as my third example let us see what was going on in 1954 in Central America that interested Canada. The record shows that in 1954 Guatemala got over $16,000 worth of ammunition from Canada. In the preceding year they got only $172 worth. That caught my attention and I wondered what in the world had happened in Guatemala. I looked into it and found that things were in a rather disturbed state in that country at that time. In 1953 important positions in the government had come under the control of the communists and in January, February and March of 1954 shipments of arms reached that country from Canada. But the Russians did it on a proper scale. When they play they play for high stakes, and a whole shipload totalling 2,000 tons of military supplies which were loaded at Stettin in Poland, ostensibly headed for Africa, reached Guatemala. Of course then the neighbouring states had to interest themselves in the problem, there was intervention in Guatemala, the government was overthrown and the situation was restored.
In 1954 Canada supplied $25,000 worth of ammunition to Costa Rica, which is not far away, $30,000 odd worth to Cuba and $15,000 worth to Panama. So in the year 1954 we find from the operation of the export permit system of this government that the Canadian government supplied ammunition to a communist controlled government in Guatemala. I think the committee might very well investigate the method by which our ammunition is disposed of.
I would like to ask this question. What is the final disposition of this ammunition? Has it been re-exported? Has it perhaps ended
Shipment of Arms Abroad up in communist hands in Malaya or Indochina? Has it perhaps ended up in the hands of some of the Mau Mau tribesmen of Kenya, or is it now in the hands of Algerian tribesmen? Once ammunition is exported to a world market without any effective control over its re-export, the most disastrous things may happen. It surely is shameful to think-and I hope a committee of inquiry shows otherwise-that perhaps Canadian-manufactured ammunition has fallen into the hands of people who with that ammunition will kill British and Australian troops in Malaya or French legionnaires in Algeria.
Those are some of the reasons I can advance for the need of a committee to examine our method in dealing with these modern and dangerous weapons. Ammunition does not become obsolete. The Hotchkiss, the Lewis, the Vickers, perhaps the Bren, are now considered obsolete and have been superseded by the Browning machine gun, but those same guns in the hands of men who are bent on fighting would be just as effective as they were 20 or 30 years ago, when they were considered modern and dangerous.
Canada has got itself into a very peculiar position with regard to trafficking in arms. The only way we can find out whether or not we are permitting the export of destructive weapons is by an investigation. An investigation would show whether our tinkering with military supplies to countries that are not our allies and are not engaged in assisting us against the one major opponent is not likely to do more to foment trouble and strife rather than to maintain peace.
What in the world has happened to the millions of rounds of ammunition sent down to Central America, the Caribbean and South America? Who knows now where that has gone? Perhaps it has made its way over to the sensitive area in the Middle East or some other sensitive area. Then what is going to be the outcome of this reckless disregard, as it appears to me, in handling that type of equipment? In the final analysis, trouble will break out somewhere and Canadian troops will be required to take some action. That is what may happen, and by all means we should resist and oppose anything like that happening.
We can only check the danger by a thorough investigation here in the House of Commons. We cannot do it by questions and answers on the orders of the day. That has been proven over the past three weeks. We can do it only by a thorough investigation. Such an investigation, laying before the committee and finally before the house the facts of the matter, will give us an indication as

Shipment of Arms Abroad,
to whether or not there has been any properly controlled policy or method of procedure on the part of the government. At the moment I think that the matter is completely out of control, and I think dollars have been the consideration.
I do not know how the moral aspect of it could be investigated, but we have had a new moral principle brought forward for our attention, to the effect that if a number of larger nations ship arms to an area where there is tension, it is not morally wrong for Canada to do so as well. That would be a nice question for our moral philosophers to deal with. Right or wrong is not to be determined by the morals involved but by numbers. It is an exercise in numerology. If we are not going to indulge in an arms race or permit other countries to engage in an arms race, as the Prime Minister pointed out today, how do we prevent it? How do we balance arms and ammunition against arms and ammunition? Do five hundred guns equal 500 guns? How many anti-aircraft guns equal one airplane? That is an impossible basis. There are so many other factors that have to be considered; the supply of ammunition, in which Canada is very active, the training of troops, leadership and morale.
In playing this game we are like children in a kindergarten piling up building blocks to see how high we can get them before they topple over. In supplying arms to both sides, Canada has got itself into a very awkward position, and only a thorough investigation by a committee of this house would determine whether or not the method of procedure of the government is sound and proper.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I be allowed to tell the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and those who will follow him in the discussion of the amendment he announced earlier that there appears to me, judging by the tenor of his arguments and the words used in his speech today, a very close relationship to the debate that took place not very long ago on a motion of want of confidence, moved when the debate on external affairs was arranged. He does not come to the same conclusion by his amendment, but perhaps we might have a debate which is not so repetitious of the one that took place the other day if arguments were directed more closely to the purport of the amendment he intends to move, and about which he spoke earlier.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to bring my remarks to a conclusion in a very few minutes. Before the dinner hour I was dealing with the subject of the shipment from Canada of arms, ammunition and military equipment generally. I questioned the effectiveness of the present system of export permits in controlling those shipments. I gave just a few examples. The amounts of money involved are small in relation to the cost of airplanes and tanks. I was dealing with the cost of ammunition. Ammunition is cheap, but it is ammunition that kills.
To those who are impressed by size, let me say that a battalion of infantry attempting to cross 400 or 500 yards of open ground against a battery of 25-pounder or 105 millimetre guns-and those are terribly destructive weapons of war of great size-would have a greater chance of surviving and reaching its objective than if crossing the open ground against four machine guns properly sighted for cross-fire and firing small ammunition. Under our present system of export permits we are placing millions of rounds of small arms ammunition in the hands of men here and there throughout the world in order that they may kill each other.
I have urged that for the purpose of securing the necessary information in order that the house may make a decision, the whole matter should be referred to a committee. This is a method to which I am sure there is no objection, and the government may wish to adopt the suggestion in order that full information may be made available to the public. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan):
That the motion be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the word "That" and substituting therefor the following:
"in the opinion of this house, the procedure with respect to the issuing of permits for the export of arms, ammunition, and military equipment, should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs with instructions to consider and to recommend to this house a definite code of procedure with respect thereto.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that I am going to support the amendment, because I feel that after the discussions that have taken place in the house over the last few weeks there is considerable uneasiness in various parts of the country with respect to Canada's exports of munitions of war.
I am not suggesting that at the present time Canada is fomenting trouble anywhere in the world. That, I think, is not the intention either of the mover of the amendment or his

party. But I think it is wise that the house and the country should understand the procedures involved in the issue of permits for the export of munitions. We know very well that permits are not required for the export of war material to our allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Nor, I take it, is it the intention of the mover that we shall divulge to what extent we are supporting our sister nations of the commonwealth in the securing of the necessary arms and so on in order to defend themselves and our way of life if they or that way of life should be attacked.
But over the last few weeks we have had considerable discussion in the house, and many questions have been asked, regarding the export of airplanes, ammunition and guns by permit through private organizations. I have a very vivid recollection over the years of discussions in the house and throughout the country regarding the activities of these private companies. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think they are no more scrupulous in their activities today than they were in days gone by when they were so frequently called, as they were the other evening by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), merchants of death.
I have noticed some of their activities in our own country over the last year or two. I was very annoyed, for example, by a photograph that appeared as an advertisement by Canadair in Time magazine, other magazines and some of the newspapers of this country. It so happens that I am a member of the church which was photographed and used in the advertisement. It is one of the largest churches of my denomination in the city of Ottawa. I refer to St. Matthew's church. The photograph in the advertisement showed a few people scattered throughout the church, and the implication was that we were not prepared either spiritually or through armaments to defend our way of life against communism. In fact that was the tenor of the advertising around the picture of this particular church and its interior.
The story of the photograph is rather interesting. Canadair secured the services of a well-known photographer. The church authorities did not know why the photograph was going to be taken. Canadair got about 20 elderly people from one of the homes in the city, took them to the church scattered them throughout the church so as to make it appear that the church was habitually empty when people were called to worship there. Yet I can testify-

On a week day?
