It is not given to many of us to look far into the future, but of this no one who observes your country from outside can doubt a future, an almost unimaginably great future, is in your hands. I have no doubt that you will fashion it in a manner worthy of a great people.
And so, Mr. Speakers, I salute this Canada which commands the future as probably no other land in the world today. I salute you also as the standard bearer of loyalty and a herald of good will. And I wish you well.

On behalf of the Senate of Canada may I say to you, Mr. Prime Minister, how greatly we appreciate your visit to Canada, your courtesy in meeting with us and, on their behalf, may I thank you for the address you have just delivered.
We will never forget the gigantic effort and sacrifice that the people of the United Kingdom made in the cause of freedom; their contribution in the rebuilding of a war-torn world and their efforts in building a better future.
The attendant circumstances of your visit, Mr. Prime Minister, are evidence of the leadership you are continuing to show in this respect. I need hardly say that in the peculiar position Canada occupies in relation in particular to the United Kingdom and the United States and, in general, to the other countries that are signatories to the North Atlantic treaty, we welcome every effort that is made towards greater understanding and in the achieving of a common viewpoint. Your very presence here and in Washington is evidence that you are keenly alive to the inestimable value of personal contacts in helping to attain these ends.
We would particularly ask you, Mr. Prime Minister, to convey our greetings to the members of the United Kingdom parliament. We hold them in the greatest respect, but we see far too little of each other. If it were possible to develop something more of the personal relationship and understanding between the members of our respective legislatures that already exist and are being constantly developed between the executive and administrative branches of government, not only would the attendant benefit be inestimable but it is quite possible that the difficulties of those whose responsibility it is to initiate policies might be lessened accordingly.
We wish you well in your undertakings. May divine Providence bless your endeavours.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Honoured guests, Mr. Prime Minister, hon. members of the Senate,

hon. members of the House of Commons, ladies and gentlemen:
(Translation) :
Once a well-known American writer, Nicholas Murray Butler, pointing out the multitudinous problems peculiar to the twentieth century, stressed the high ability required of the men called upon to solve those problems. Then again, another distinguished American author, Whittier, said: "Each crisis brings its words and deeds".
These words naturally come to mind at this time when it is my very great privilege to thank you, Mr. Prime Minister, for your interesting speech and your kindly presence among us. May I be allowed to add that the success of your career arouses in us the deepest admiration.
I should fear to lapse into the commonplace in repeating that Sir Anthony Eden, "the specialist in foreign affairs, the virtuoso of diplomacy", to use the words of his biographer, Campbell-Johnson, is a statesman of the highest intellectual standing who has always shown supreme ability and understanding in tackling the most difficult international problems.
At the general elections, in 1950, he summed up his political creed by referring to the theory of the three unities; first, the unity that should exist within the commonwealth; second, the unity of western Europe; and third, the unity which, across the Atlantic, binds England to the United States. Today he has restated his political faith in those three unities and has added two others which are most important and inseparable from the first three.
We believe, as he does, in maintaining a friendly solidarity between the countries which make up the commonwealth.
For us, who are French-speaking and whose mother country was France, we cannot forget, sir, that you have always been a friend of that great nation, that you have, on many occasions, revived the principles that made a success of the Entente Cordiale. You have always believed that the solidarity of Anglo-French relations, nay of western European relations, was the very basis of relations between all western European countries, not only for the present but also for the future.
There are, of course, "other places under the sun" and, as a North American people, we rejoice at your relations with the United States. On the occasion of your visit to America in 1943, President Roosevelt was able to say that you both seemed to agree on approximately ninety-five per cent of the

problems, which is a remarkable proportion. And in the last few days, you and the present President of the United States have just agreed one hundred per cent on the definition of the philosophy behind our way of life, as you personally chose to call it, a definition which was incorporated in this henceforth memorable document, the declaration of Washington.
This is consistent with the objective which is yours today and which you set yourself a long time ago when you said in the House of Commons:
I am convinced that a closer understanding between our nation and the United States constitutes the most important objective that the government of that country could propose to us.
Visit of Sir Anthony Eden
In addition you have accomplished a tour de force, as it were, in bringing about an effective rapprochement with new Germany.
As I said just now, each crisis brings its words and deeds, and brings forth the indispensable men whose courage and logic carry ideals into the realm of reality.
(Text) :
Each crisis brings its words and deeds; it' brings also to the fore the men to utter those words and to do those deeds, and men with sufficient courage and consistency to translate their ideals into realities. Of such a breed is our honoured guest today.
So, in the name of the House of Commons and of the Canadian people, may I say to you, sir: Thank you and good luck!

Tuesday, February 7, 1956
